say: You give it a rate for one period, such as a yearly rate. It gives back the **equivalent** rate for a different period, such as a month.
The key idea: growth multiplies. Twelve months of growth at rate $i$ must give the same result as one year at the annual rate, so $(1+i)^{12} = 1 + \text{annual rate}$.

how.higher: It appears as a part of its own or a short step in the loan and savings questions on Paper 1, in 2015, 2017, 2023 and 2024, worth 5 to 10 marks.

example.question: A bank quotes an annual percentage rate (APR) of $3.6\%$. Find the equivalent monthly rate, correct to 3 significant figures.

steps.title: Set up the equation
steps.say: One year is $12$ months. Growth at the monthly rate $\hl{1}{i}$ twelve times must equal the growth at the annual rate.

steps.title: Take the 12th root
steps.say: To undo the power of $12$, raise both sides to the power $\frac{1}{12}$.

steps.title: Subtract 1
steps.say: Take away the $1$ to leave $\hl{1}{i}$ alone, then write it as a percentage.

higher.tip: Write the formula and start substituting. Marks are given for the correct formula and for some substitution, even if the rest goes wrong.
Use the right root. The power is the number of periods in a year, so a monthly rate needs $12$ and a quarterly rate needs $4$. Using the wrong one loses marks.
Give the rate as a percentage, not a decimal. A decimal answer loses a mark.

say: You give it a gross pay, the tax rates and bands, and the tax credits. It gives back the **gross tax**, the **net tax** and the **net pay**.
The key idea: each rate applies only to its own slice of the pay, and the tax credits come off the tax, not off the pay.

how.higher: It was a part of its own in 2024, Paper 1 Q7(a), worth 10 marks, with a tax credit and two rates.
how.ordinary: It is a main skill almost every year on Paper 1, usually the first parts of a money question, worth 5 to 15 marks, often with USC and PRSI as well.

example.question: Ciara earns $€56\,000$ a year. She pays tax at $20\%$ on the first $€42\,000$ and $40\%$ on the rest. Her tax credits are $€3\,500$. Find her net pay.

steps.title: Tax at the 20% rate
steps.say: The $20\%$ rate applies only to the first $€42\,000$.

steps.title: Tax at the 40% rate
steps.say: The rest of the pay is what is left after the first $€42\,000$. Tax that at $40\%$.

steps.title: Add to get gross tax
steps.say: Add the two amounts to get the $\hl{1}{\text{gross tax}}$.

steps.title: Take off the credits
steps.say: The credits come off the tax. What is left is the $\hl{2}{\text{net tax}}$.

steps.title: Find the net pay
steps.say: Take the $\hl{2}{\text{net tax}}$ from the gross pay.

lines.text: Only the tax is reduced by the credits. The pay is not.

ordinary.tip: Write the rate against each slice of pay, such as $0.2 \times 35300$. Using the rates earns marks even if the sum goes wrong.
Find the tax at each rate separately, then add them to get the gross tax. Each step has its own mark.
Subtract the tax credit from the gross tax to get the net tax. Show both numbers.

sources.quote: Correctly handles gross tax and tax credits

ordinary.tip: For USC, write each rate with its own slice of income. Setting up every rate correctly earns the High Partial Credit.

sources.quote: Correct formulation of all 3 USC rates

say: You give it a job: the amounts of materials, the price of each, the wastage and the labour. It gives back the **total cost**.
The key idea: cost each part of the job on its own, then add them. Wastage means buying more than you need, so the amount goes up by that percentage.

how.higher: It is rare at higher level. It appeared once, in 2017 Paper 1 Q8(b)(vi).
how.ordinary: It is a main skill in most years, on both papers, as a part of a longer question on building, painting or flooring a space, worth 5 to 20 marks.

example.question: A room is $5$ m by $4$ m. The floor is to be tiled. Tiles cost $€30$ per m², and $8\%$ extra is bought for wastage. The tiler charges $€45$ per hour for $6$ hours. Find the total cost.

steps.title: Area of the floor
steps.say: Multiply the length by the width.

steps.title: Add the wastage
steps.say: $8\%$ extra means $108\%$ of the area. Multiply by $1.08$.

steps.title: Cost of the tiles
steps.say: Multiply the area to buy by the price per m². This is the cost of the $\hl{1}{\text{tiles}}$.

steps.title: Cost of the labour
steps.say: Multiply the hours by the rate per hour to get the $\hl{2}{\text{labour}}$.

ordinary.tip: Work out each cost on its own line. Marks are given for any one cost element shown.
Find every element before you add VAT or any other percentage. The total is worked out from all of them together.
If you use an answer from an earlier part, say so and show it. Any use of it earns marks.
Round money as the question asks. An incorrect or missing rounding costs a mark.

sources.quote: Apply F* if incorrect or no rounding

say: You give it an estimated value and the true value. It gives back the **percentage error**: how far off the estimate is, as a percentage of the truth.
The key idea: the error is the difference between the two values, and you always divide it by the **true** value.

how.higher: It appeared as a step in 2015 Paper 1 Q3(b) and 2025 Paper 2 Q8(b), worth about 10 marks and following an area or angle calculation.
how.ordinary: It is a main skill in 2017 and 2022 to 2025 on Paper 1, usually a short part worth 5 to 10 marks after an area or reading from a graph.

example.question: A table is measured as $1.46$ m long. The true length is $1.50$ m. Find the percentage error, correct to one decimal place.

steps.title: Find the error
steps.say: The error is the difference between the true value and the estimate.

steps.title: Divide by the true value
steps.say: Divide the $\hl{1}{\text{error}}$ by the true value, $1.50$. Multiply by $100$ to make it a percentage.

steps.title: Round the answer
steps.say: Round to one decimal place and write the percent sign.

higher.tip: Find the percentage error with the true value on the bottom. A correct formula earns marks by itself.
Write the answer as a percentage. Leaving off the percent sign loses marks.

sources.quote: Answer not given as a percentage

higher.tip: Round as asked. An answer with no rounding or the wrong rounding loses a mark.

ordinary.tip: Write the percentage error formula down first. It earns marks on its own.
Show the error and the true value separately. The top and the bottom of the fraction are each worth marks.
Round as asked. No rounding or the wrong rounding loses a mark.

sources.quote: Apply a * for no or incorrect rounding
